q: How fast is CO2 in the atmosphere rising?

queries.purpose: Yearly rise in atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa, last 30 years
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(co2_ppm - LAG(co2_ppm) OVER (ORDER BY year), 2) AS value FROM co2_annual QUALIFY year >= (SELECT MAX(year) FROM co2_annual) - 29 ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average yearly rise in CO2 by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(decade AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(diff), 2) AS value FROM (SELECT year, (year // 10) * 10 AS decade, co2_ppm - LAG(co2_ppm) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS diff FROM co2_annual) WHERE diff IS NOT NULL GROUP BY decade ORDER BY decade LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Annual mean CO2 level, every 5 years
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(co2_ppm, 1) AS value FROM co2_annual WHERE year % 5 = 0 OR year = (SELECT MAX(year) FROM co2_annual) ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

story.lead: CO2 is rising faster than ever, about 2.7 ppm a year
story.summary: The air's CO2 level rose **2.74 ppm** in 2025, and **3.53 ppm** in 2024, the biggest jump in the last 30 years. The yearly rise in the 2020s averages **2.62 ppm**, about **three times** the 1960s pace of **0.86 ppm**. The total has gone from 316.9 ppm in 1960 to **427.4 ppm** in 2025.
story.sub: Yearly average CO2 measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (NOAA), 1959 to 2025. ppm means parts per million: molecules of CO2 per million molecules of air.

facts.label: CO2 level in 2025, up from 316.9 in 1960

points.h: Each year adds more CO2, and recent years add the most
points.p: The rise varies from year to year. It was as low as **1.14 ppm** in 1997 and as high as **3.53 ppm** in 2024. Since 2016, no year has risen by less than about 2 ppm.

points.h: The yearly rise has tripled since the 1960s
points.p: The average yearly rise grew in almost every decade, from **0.86 ppm** in the 1960s to **2.4 ppm** in the 2010s. The 2020s figure of **2.62 ppm** covers 2020 to 2025 only. The 1990s were the one small dip, at 1.53 against 1.64 in the 1980s.

points.h: CO2 has climbed from 317 to 427 ppm since 1960
points.p: The level rose **29.5 ppm** in the 25 years from 1960 to 1985. It then rose **37.3 ppm** in just the 15 years from 2010 to 2025. The climb is getting steeper.

story.note: These are yearly averages from one station in Hawaii, which is used as a measure of the whole atmosphere. The 2020s decade average covers 2020 to 2025 only.

q: Which countries have the biggest economies?

queries.purpose: Top 15 economies by GDP in 2023 (current US dollars)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, round(gdp_usd/1e12, 2) AS value FROM gdp WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2023 AND gdp_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY gdp_usd DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Top 15 economies by GDP per person in 2023 among countries with over 10 million people
queries.sql: SELECT g.country AS label, round(g.gdp_usd/p.population) AS value FROM gdp g JOIN population p ON g.country_code = p.country_code AND g.year = p.year WHERE NOT g.is_aggregate AND g.year = 2023 AND g.gdp_usd IS NOT NULL AND p.population > 10000000 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Top 10 economies by GDP in 2000 for comparison (current US dollars)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, round(gdp_usd/1e12, 2) AS value FROM gdp WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2000 AND gdp_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY gdp_usd DESC LIMIT 10

story.lead: The United States and China dominate the world's economies.
story.summary: In 2023 the United States had the biggest economy at **$27.36 trillion**, with China next at **$17.79 trillion**. Together they are far ahead of Germany in third place at $4.46 trillion. China's economy has grown about **15 times** bigger since 2000.
story.sub: World Bank GDP in current US dollars, 2023 compared with 2000; population for per-person figures, 2023.

facts.label: US economy in 2023, the world's biggest
US output per person, highest of larger countries

points.h: The US and China are far ahead of everyone else
points.p: The US economy was **$27.36 trillion** in 2023 and China's was **$17.79 trillion**. Germany, third, was **$4.46 trillion**, so China is about four times bigger than Germany. India ranked fifth at $3.55 trillion.

points.h: Per person, the US still leads, but China is not on the list
points.p: Among countries with over 10 million people, the US had **$81,249** of output per person. Australia was next at **$64,660**. China and India are in the top 15 by total size but not on this list.

points.h: In 2000, China was only sixth biggest
points.p: In 2000 China's economy was **$1.21 trillion**, behind the US, Japan, Germany, the UK and France. By 2023 it was **$17.79 trillion**. Japan was second in 2000 at $4.97 trillion and was fourth in 2023 at $4.21 trillion.

story.note: These are current US dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so growth since 2000 includes rising prices. GDP per person only covers countries with over 10 million people.

q: How much has the world warmed?

queries.purpose: Global temperature anomaly by decade (NASA GISTEMP, above the 1951-1980 average)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(CAST(floor(year/10)*10 AS INTEGER) AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, round(avg(anomaly_c), 2) AS value FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP' GROUP BY floor(year/10) ORDER BY floor(year/10)

queries.purpose: Yearly anomaly over the last 30 years (NASA GISTEMP)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(anomaly_c, 2) AS value FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP' AND year >= (SELECT max(year) - 29 FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP') ORDER BY year

queries.purpose: Ten warmest years on record (NASA GISTEMP)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(anomaly_c, 2) AS value FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP' ORDER BY anomaly_c DESC LIMIT 10

story.lead: The world is about 1.2°C warmer than in 1951–1980.
story.summary: NASA's record shows 2025 was **1.19°C** above the 1951–1980 average. The 2020s so far average **1.07°C** above it, compared with **-0.22°C** in the 1880s. That is a rise of about **1.3°C** between those two decades.
story.sub: NASA GISTEMP global surface temperature, 1880–2025, compared with the 1951–1980 average.

facts.label: 2023, 2024 and 2025 are the three warmest years

points.h: Each decade has been warmer than the last since the 1970s
points.p: Decades hovered below or near the 1951–1980 average until the 1970s (**0.03°C**). Since then every decade has been warmer, reaching **1.07°C** in the 2020s so far. The 2020s are about **0.26°C** warmer than the 2010s.

points.h: Recent years have jumped well above the late 1990s
points.p: In 1996 the world was **0.33°C** above the average. By 2024 it was **1.29°C**. The last three years (2023–2025) were all above **1.15°C**, higher than any year before 2023.

points.h: The ten warmest years are all from 2015 onward
points.p: All ten of the warmest years on record fall between 2015 and 2025. The top three are **2024**, 2025 and 2023. Only 2021 is missing from that stretch.

story.note: These are differences from the 1951–1980 average, not from the 1800s, so the total warming since early industrial times is larger than these figures suggest.

q: How much have US house prices risen?

queries.purpose: US national home price index by year (January 2000 = 100), annual average
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG("index"), 1) AS value FROM us_house_prices WHERE area = 'US national' AND year(month) < 2026 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Percent rise in home prices since Jan 1987 vs latest month, by metro and national
queries.sql: WITH f AS (SELECT area, arg_min("index", month) AS first_v, arg_max("index", month) AS last_v FROM us_house_prices WHERE area NOT IN ('20-city composite','10-city composite') GROUP BY area) SELECT regexp_replace(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-', '') AS label, ROUND((last_v / first_v - 1) * 100, 0) AS value FROM f ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: US national index at January each year since 2000 vs January 2000 base
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND("index", 1) AS value FROM us_house_prices WHERE area = 'US national' AND month(month) = 1 AND year(month) >= 2000 ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

story.lead: US home prices are up more than fivefold since 1987
story.summary: Across the US, home prices are **429%** higher than in January 1987, which means about **5.3 times** the price. Since January 2000 they have more than tripled, to **326.8** on a scale where 2000 equals 100. The climb was not smooth: prices fell about a quarter after 2007 before rising again.
story.sub: S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller home price index, January 1987 to July 2026 (US national), not adjusted for inflation.

facts.label: US national rise, Jan 1987 to Jul 2026
fall from Jan 2007 peak to Jan 2012 low

points.h: Prices rose, peaked in 2006, then fell for five years
points.p: This chart shows only 1987 to 2016. The yearly average went from **66.3** in 1987 to a peak of **183.5** in 2006. It then slid to **139.2** in 2011, and by 2016 it was back near the old peak at **180.9**.

points.h: West Coast cities have risen the most since 1987
points.p: San Diego (**724%**), Portland (**714%**) and San Francisco (**696%**) lead the list, ahead of the US national figure of **429%**. Dallas is lowest at **197%**. Metros started at different dates, so the periods are not all the same.

points.h: Prices more than tripled since 2000, after a long dip
points.p: In January terms, the index reached **182.7** in 2007, fell to **134.2** in 2012, then climbed to **326.8** in 2026. That is about **2.4 times** the 2012 low. The rise from 2025 to 2026 was small, just 3.2 points.

story.note: These are prices in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the rise is general price growth. Some metros start later than 1987, so their percentages cover shorter periods.

q: How have oil prices changed since 2000?

queries.purpose: Average Brent crude price per year since 2000
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_barrel), 1) AS value FROM oil_prices WHERE benchmark = 'Brent' AND year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Highest monthly Brent price in each year since 2000
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(MAX(usd_per_barrel), 1) AS value FROM oil_prices WHERE benchmark = 'Brent' AND year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average WTI price per year since 2000, for comparison with Brent
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_barrel), 1) AS value FROM oil_prices WHERE benchmark = 'WTI' AND year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

story.lead: Oil prices roughly tripled, with big swings along the way.
story.summary: A barrel of Brent crude averaged **$28.5** in 2000 and **$90.6** so far in 2026, about **three times** as much in current dollars. The path was bumpy: prices peaked near **$112** in 2012, then fell to **$43.5** in 2016. A barrel is a standard oil measure of about 159 litres.
story.sub: Monthly Brent and WTI crude oil spot prices (US EIA), 2000 to 2026 so far, in nominal US dollars per barrel.

facts.label: Average Brent price per barrel, 2000 vs 2026 so far
Highest monthly Brent price so far in 2026

points.h: Yearly average price climbed, crashed, and climbed again
points.p: Brent averaged **$28.5** in 2000 and rose to **$111.7** in 2012. It dropped to **$43.5** in 2016, recovered to $71.1 in 2018, then fell to **$41.8** in 2020. It hit **$100.8** in 2022 and stands at **$90.6** so far in 2026.

points.h: Monthly peaks show even sharper spikes
points.p: The highest single month was **$132.7** in 2008, while the 2008 yearly average was only **$96.8**. In 2026 so far, the top month is **$117.3**, well above the year's average of **$90.6**. That means prices have moved a lot within single years.

points.h: US benchmark WTI follows the same path, usually lower
points.p: WTI, the main US oil price, averaged **$30.3** in 2000 and **$83.4** so far in 2026. In most years it sat below Brent, for example **$94.8** against **$100.8** in 2022. The gap was widest in 2012, at **$94.1** against **$111.7**.

story.note: Prices are in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, and 2026 is only part of a year.

q: Is the sea level rising faster?

queries.purpose: Pace of rise per decade, tide-gauge reconstruction (CSIRO), 1880s-2000s
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, round(regr_slope(csiro_inches, year) * 10, 2) AS value FROM sea_level WHERE csiro_inches IS NOT NULL AND year <= 2009 GROUP BY year // 10 ORDER BY year // 10

queries.purpose: Pace of rise in the satellite era (NOAA), by period
queries.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN year <= 2002 THEN '1993-2002' WHEN year <= 2012 THEN '2003-2012' ELSE '2013-2023' END AS label, round(regr_slope(noaa_inches, year) * 10, 2) AS value FROM sea_level WHERE noaa_inches IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY min(year)

queries.purpose: Total rise since 1880 at the start of each decade (CSIRO)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(csiro_inches, 2) AS value FROM sea_level WHERE csiro_inches IS NOT NULL AND year % 10 = 0 ORDER BY year

story.lead: Yes, sea level is rising faster now.
story.summary: Sea level rose about **8.8 inches** between 1880 and 2010, and the recent pace is the quickest on record. In the 2000s it rose **1.45 inches per decade**, about twice the typical earlier pace. Satellites show **1.54 inches per decade** for 2013-2023, up from **0.96** in 2003-2012.
story.sub: US EPA sea level data: tide-gauge reconstruction (CSIRO) 1880-2013 and satellites (NOAA) 1993-2023.

points.h: The 2000s had the fastest decade in the long record
points.p: Tide gauges show the pace jumping around from decade to decade, from almost no change to about 0.8 inches per decade. The 2000s stand out at **1.45 inches per decade**, the highest of all 13 decades. The 1990s were also high at **0.85**.

points.h: Satellites show a speed-up after 2012
points.p: Satellites measured **1.06 inches per decade** in 1993-2002 and **0.96** in 2003-2012. In 2013-2023 the pace rose to **1.54 inches per decade**, about 60% faster than the decade before.

points.h: The total rise has added up to almost 9 inches
points.p: By 2010 the sea was **8.83 inches** higher than in 1880. The 2000s alone added about **1.77 inches**, more than the first two decades together (**1.13 inches** by 1900). The satellite and tide-gauge records use different baselines, so they should not be added together.

story.note: Pace is the slope of a straight line through each period's yearly values. The tide-gauge record ends in 2013 and the satellite record starts in 1993, so they overlap only partly.

q: What is the US unemployment rate over time?

queries.purpose: US unemployment rate by year, 1947-2025 (annual average, % of labour force)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(unemployment_rate_pct, 1) AS value FROM us_employment WHERE year >= 1947 ORDER BY year LIMIT 30 OFFSET 0

queries.purpose: Average US unemployment rate by decade (percent of labour force)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(unemployment_rate_pct), 1) AS value FROM us_employment WHERE year >= 1950 GROUP BY (year // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Share of the population with a job (employment-population ratio), by decade average
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(employment_population_ratio_pct), 1) AS value FROM us_employment WHERE year >= 1950 GROUP BY (year // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

story.lead: US unemployment has moved in waves, not one trend
story.summary: The share of US workers without a job has gone up and down since 1947. The decade average peaked in the 1980s at **7.3%**, up from **4.5%** in the 1950s, and is **4.8%** in the 2020s so far. In the early years shown, it ranged from **2.9%** in 1953 to **8.5%** in 1975.
story.sub: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, annual averages. The year-by-year chart shows 1947-1976 only; decade averages cover 1950-2025.

facts.label: Share of people with a job, 2020s

points.h: Unemployment jumped in bad years, then fell back, 1947-1976
points.p: This chart shows only the first 30 years. The rate swung between **2.9%** in 1953 and **8.5%** in 1975, nearly three times as high. It rose sharply in 1949, 1954, 1958, 1961, 1970 and 1975, then eased in the years after.

points.h: The 1980s had the highest average unemployment
points.p: Averaged by decade, unemployment rose from **4.5%** in the 1950s to **7.3%** in the 1980s. It then fell to **5.5%** in the 2000s, rose to **6.2%** in the 2010s, and is **4.8%** in the 2020s so far (2020-2025).

points.h: The share of people with a job peaked in the 1990s
points.p: This counts everyone of working age, not just those looking for work. The share with a job climbed from **56.6%** in the 1950s to **62.8%** in the 1990s. It has since fallen to **59.2%** in the 2020s, which is **3.6** points lower than the 1990s peak.

story.note: The unemployment rate is the share of people in the labour force (working or looking for work) who have no job; the 2020s average covers 2020-2025 only.

sources: 2.8 points not used; nearly three times: 8.5 / 2.9 = 2.9 (1975 = 8.5, 1953 = 2.9)

q: How much has gold gone up?

queries.purpose: Gold price by decade (average, nominal US dollars per ounce)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year(month) // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_ounce), 0) AS value FROM gold_prices WHERE year(month) >= 1900 GROUP BY (year(month) // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year(month) // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average gold price per year since 2000 (nominal US dollars, 2026 so far)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_ounce), 0) AS value FROM gold_prices WHERE year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Gold price at the start of selected years vs latest month (nominal US dollars)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(month, '%b %Y') AS label, ROUND(usd_per_ounce, 0) AS value FROM gold_prices WHERE (month IN (SELECT MIN(month) FROM gold_prices WHERE year(month) IN (1900,1925,1950,1971,1980,2000,2010,2020) GROUP BY year(month))) OR month = (SELECT MAX(month) FROM gold_prices) ORDER BY month LIMIT 30

story.lead: Gold now costs about 230 times its 1900 price.
story.summary: An ounce of gold cost **$19** in January 1900 and **$4,319** in September 2026. That is about **230 times** higher, in current dollars. Since January 2000 the price has risen about **15 times**, from $284.
story.sub: Monthly gold prices in nominal US dollars per troy ounce, 1900 to September 2026 (2026 is a partial year).

points.h: Gold sat near $35 for decades, then took off
points.p: Average prices stayed between **$19** and **$36** an ounce through the 1960s. The 1970s average was **$132**, and the 2020s average so far is **$2,453**. That is about 70 times the 1960s level.

points.h: The yearly average has more than doubled since 2022
points.p: The average rose from **$279** in 2000 to **$1,670** in 2012. It then slipped to **$1,161** in 2015. Since 2022 ($1,801) it has climbed to **$4,552** so far in 2026.

points.h: Gold has jumped since 1971, with one big spike in 1980
points.p: Gold was **$38** in January 1971 and **$675** in January 1980. In January 2000 it was back down at **$284**. The latest month, September 2026, is **$4,319**.

story.note: These are current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the rise just reflects higher prices in general.

How did gold prices compare with inflation in the 1970s?

queries.purpose: GDP in 2023 as a multiple of 2000 (current US dollars), economies of at least $10bn in 2000
queries.sql: SELECT g23.country AS label, round(g23.gdp_usd / g00.gdp_usd, 1) AS value FROM gdp g00 JOIN gdp g23 ON g00.country_code = g23.country_code AND g00.year = 2000 AND g23.year = 2023 WHERE NOT g00.is_aggregate AND g00.gdp_usd >= 1e10 AND g23.gdp_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Biggest total GDP gain 2000 to 2023 (billions of current US dollars)
queries.sql: SELECT g23.country AS label, round((g23.gdp_usd - g00.gdp_usd) / 1e9) AS value FROM gdp g00 JOIN gdp g23 ON g00.country_code = g23.country_code AND g00.year = 2000 AND g23.year = 2023 WHERE NOT g00.is_aggregate AND g23.gdp_usd IS NOT NULL AND g00.gdp_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Fastest population growth 2000 to 2025 (percent), countries with at least 1 million people in 2000
queries.sql: SELECT p25.country AS label, round((p25.population * 1.0 / p00.population - 1) * 100) AS value FROM population p00 JOIN population p25 ON p00.country_code = p25.country_code AND p00.year = 2000 AND p25.year = 2025 WHERE NOT p00.is_aggregate AND p00.population >= 1000000 AND p25.population IS NOT NULL ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

story.lead: China, Kazakhstan and Viet Nam grew fastest since 2000.
story.summary: Measured by the size of their economies, China's GDP was **14.7 times** larger in 2023 than in 2000, just ahead of Kazakhstan (**14.3**) and Viet Nam (**13.8**). In dollar terms, only the United States added a similar amount to China: **$17.1 trillion** against **$16.6 trillion**. These figures are in current US dollars, so they include price rises.
story.sub: World Bank GDP in current US dollars, 2000 to 2023; World Bank population, 2000 to 2025.

facts.label: United Arab Emirates' population growth, 2000 to 2025

points.h: China, Kazakhstan and Viet Nam grew about 14-fold
points.p: Among economies worth at least $10 billion in 2000, China's output grew to **14.7 times** its 2000 size. Kazakhstan (**14.3**) and Viet Nam (**13.8**) were close behind. Romania, in fourth place, reached **9.4 times**.

points.h: The US and China added the most dollars
points.p: The United States added about **$17,110 billion** and China about **$16,583 billion**. India was third with **$3,082 billion**, less than a fifth of either. Fast growth in multiples and big gains in dollars are not the same thing.

points.h: Gulf and African countries grew their populations fastest
points.p: The United Arab Emirates' population grew by **230%** between 2000 and 2025, so it was about three times its 2000 size. Kuwait grew **149%**, Chad **147%** and Niger **143%**. This list covers people, not money.

story.note: GDP is in current US dollars, not adjusted for inflation, and chart 1 only includes economies of at least $10 billion in 2000.

q: Where does the world's CO2 come from?

queries.purpose: 2024 CO2 emissions by source
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Oil' AS label, ROUND(liquid*3.664/1000, 1) AS value FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 'Coal', ROUND(solid*3.664/1000, 1) FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 'Natural gas', ROUND(gas*3.664/1000, 1) FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 'Cement', ROUND(cement*3.664/1000, 1) FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 'Gas flaring', ROUND(flaring*3.664/1000, 1) FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024) ORDER BY value DESC

queries.purpose: Coal's share of fossil fuel and cement CO2 by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(solid) / SUM(total_mt_carbon), 1) AS value FROM co2_emissions WHERE year >= 1900 GROUP BY year // 10 ORDER BY year // 10

queries.purpose: Average yearly total CO2 emissions by decade (2020s so far = 2020-2024)
queries.unit: billion tonnes of CO2 per year
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(total_mt_carbon) * 3.664 / 1000, 1) AS value FROM co2_emissions WHERE year >= 1900 GROUP BY year // 10 ORDER BY year // 10

story.lead: Coal is the biggest source of CO2, then oil.
story.summary: In 2024, burning coal released about **15.8 billion tonnes** of CO2, more than any other source. Oil came next at **12.5 billion tonnes**, and natural gas at **8 billion**. Together, these three fuels make up almost all of the world's fossil fuel and cement CO2.
story.sub: Global CO2 from fossil fuels and cement, Global Carbon Project; 2024, with decades from 1900 to the 2020s (2020-2024).

facts.label: coal's share of CO2 in the 2020s

points.h: Coal, oil and gas produce nearly all of the CO2
points.p: In 2024 coal gave **15.8 billion tonnes** of CO2 and oil **12.5 billion**. Natural gas gave **8 billion**. Cement (**1.5 billion**) and gas flaring (**0.4 billion**) are much smaller.

points.h: Coal's share fell sharply, then levelled off near 40%
points.p: In the 1900s coal made up **95%** of the total. By the 1970s that was down to **35.2%**. Since then it has crept back up and was **40.9%** in the 2020s.

points.h: Yearly emissions are about 15 times higher than in 1900s
points.p: The average was **2.4 billion tonnes** a year in the 1900s. It reached **37.2 billion** in 2020-2024. Growth has slowed: the rise from the 2010s to the 2020s is **1.8 billion**, against 6.5 billion from the 2000s to the 2010s.

story.note: Figures cover CO2 from fossil fuels and cement only, converted from tonnes of carbon to tonnes of CO2. The 2020s average covers 2020-2024.

q: How much ice have glaciers lost?

queries.purpose: Cumulative ice lost since 1956, by decade (metres of water equivalent)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(-cumulative_mass_balance_mwe, 1) AS value FROM glaciers WHERE year % 5 = 0 OR year = (SELECT MAX(year) FROM glaciers) ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average ice lost per year in each decade (metres of water equivalent)
queries.sql: WITH d AS (SELECT year, cumulative_mass_balance_mwe - LAG(cumulative_mass_balance_mwe) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS change FROM glaciers) SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(-AVG(change), 2) AS value FROM d WHERE change IS NOT NULL GROUP BY year // 10 ORDER BY year // 10 LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Ice lost each year over the last 20 years (metres of water equivalent)
queries.sql: WITH d AS (SELECT year, cumulative_mass_balance_mwe - LAG(cumulative_mass_balance_mwe) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS change FROM glaciers) SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(-change, 2) AS value FROM d WHERE year > (SELECT MAX(year) FROM glaciers) - 20 ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

story.lead: Glaciers have lost 29.7 metres of ice, faster lately
story.summary: Since 1956, the world's reference glaciers have lost **29.7 metres** of ice, measured as a layer of water spread over the glacier. The yearly loss is now about **five times** what it was in the 1980s. About three-quarters of all the loss has happened since 1990.
story.sub: Average of the world's reference glaciers (WGMS via US EPA), 1956 to 2023.

facts.label: lost in 2023, the most of the last 20 years
yearly loss in the 2020s vs the 1980s

points.h: The total loss keeps growing, and the line gets steeper
points.p: By 1980 the glaciers had lost **6 metres** of ice, counted as a layer of water. By 2023 the total reached **29.7 metres**. The climb is slow at first and steeper after 1990.

points.h: Since the 1980s, each decade has lost more ice per year than the last
points.p: In the 1980s glaciers lost about **0.19 metres** a year. In the 2020s so far it is about **0.97 metres** a year. That is roughly five times faster.

points.h: Every one of the last 20 years lost ice, and 2023 lost most
points.p: The yearly loss ranged from **0.38 metres** in 2008 to **1.23 metres** in 2023. The two biggest losses in this period came in the last two years, 2022 (**1.09 metres**) and 2023. No year in this stretch shows a gain.

story.note: "Metres of water equivalent" means the depth of water you would get if the lost ice were melted and spread over the glacier surface. The 2020s figure covers 2020 to 2023 only.

q: How has the euro moved against the dollar?

queries.purpose: Average euros per US dollar each year since 1999 (higher = stronger dollar; 2026 so far)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(rate), 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Highest and lowest yearly average, to show the range of the swings
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Strongest dollar month (' || strftime(month, '%b %Y') || ')' AS label, ROUND(rate, 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' ORDER BY rate DESC LIMIT 1) UNION ALL SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Weakest dollar month (' || strftime(month, '%b %Y') || ')' AS label, ROUND(rate, 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' ORDER BY rate ASC LIMIT 1) UNION ALL SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Latest month (' || strftime(month, '%b %Y') || ')' AS label, ROUND(rate, 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' ORDER BY month DESC LIMIT 1)

queries.purpose: Monthly euros per US dollar over the last 24 months
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT month AS m, strftime(month, '%b %Y') AS label, ROUND(rate, 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' ORDER BY month DESC LIMIT 24) ORDER BY m

story.lead: The euro has swung a lot, but sits mid-range now
story.summary: One US dollar bought **0.869 euros** in September 2026. That is between the extremes of **1.173** in October 2000 and **0.635** in July 2008. In everyday terms, the dollar is worth about 26% less than at its peak against the euro, and about 37% more than at its low.
story.sub: Monthly Federal Reserve exchange rates, January 1999 to September 2026 (2026 is partial).

points.h: The dollar fell against the euro until 2008, then partly recovered
points.p: In 2001 a dollar bought **1.117** euros on average. By 2008 it bought only **0.683**. Since 2015 the yearly average has stayed between about **0.85** and **0.95**, and 2026 so far is **0.861**.

points.h: The gap between the extremes is large
points.p: The dollar's best month was Oct 2000 at **1.173** euros. Its worst was Jul 2008 at **0.635**. The latest month, Sep 2026, is **0.869**, closer to the low than to the high.

points.h: Over two years the dollar dipped, then held steady
points.p: In January 2025 a dollar bought **0.966** euros. By September 2025 it bought **0.852**. Since then the rate has stayed in a narrow band from **0.846** to **0.875**.

story.note: Higher numbers mean a stronger dollar: more euros for one dollar. Before 1999 the euro did not exist, so the series starts then.

q: When was the stock market most volatile?

queries.purpose: Highest monthly VIX closes (fear index peaks)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(month, '%b %Y') AS label, ROUND(vix, 1) AS value FROM vix ORDER BY vix DESC LIMIT 12

queries.purpose: Average VIX by year
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(vix), 1) AS value FROM vix WHERE year(month) < 2026 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average VIX by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year(month) // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(vix), 1) AS value FROM vix GROUP BY (year(month) // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year(month) // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

story.lead: Fear peaked in October 2008, during the financial crisis.
story.summary: The VIX, a gauge of how nervous investors are, hit its highest month-end close in October 2008 at **59.9**. March 2020 came third at **53.5**. Yearly averages from 1990 to 2019 ranged from about **11** to **27**, so the October 2008 peak was more than twice even the most nervous year's average.
story.sub: Monthly closing values of the VIX "fear index", January 1990 to September 2026; yearly averages cover 1990 to 2019 in the chart (2026 left out as partial).

points.h: The three biggest spikes came in 2008 and 2020
points.p: The highest month-end readings were **59.9** in Oct 2008 and **55.8** in Nov 2008. March 2020 follows at **53.5**. Six of the top twelve months fall between Oct 2008 and Mar 2009, in a tight cluster.

points.h: 2008 and 2009 were the most nervous years from 1990 to 2019
points.p: Averaged over the whole year, 2009 was highest at **31.8**, just above 2008 at **31.6**. The calmest year shown was 2017 at **11.0**, about a third of the 2009 level. Late 1990s and early 2000s were also elevated, at 23 to 27.

points.h: Decade averages differ less than the spikes
points.p: The 2000s were the most nervous decade, averaging **21.9**. The 2010s were the calmest at **17.1**. The 2020s so far average **20.7**, second highest.

story.note: The VIX measures how much investors expect US stocks to swing; these are month-end closes, so a sharper spike within a month could be missed.

q: How have US interest rates changed?

queries.purpose: Average 10-year US government bond yield by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year(month) // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(yield_pct), 2) AS value FROM us_bond_yield GROUP BY (year(month) // 10) ORDER BY (year(month) // 10)

queries.purpose: Average 10-year yield each year since 1990
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(yield_pct), 2) AS value FROM us_bond_yield WHERE year(month) >= 1990 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month)

queries.purpose: Highest-yield years on record (annual average)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(yield_pct), 2) AS value FROM us_bond_yield WHERE year(month) < 2026 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 10

story.lead: US interest rates peaked in the early 1980s, then fell.
story.summary: The 10-year US government bond yield, a common measure of long-term interest rates, averaged **13.91%** a year in 1981, its highest year on record. By the 2010s the average was just **2.41%**. It has edged back up to **3.1%** in the 2020s so far.
story.sub: US 10-year government bond yield (Federal Reserve), monthly averages, April 1953 to 2026; the 2020s include 2026 so far.

facts.label: Average in the 1980s, the highest decade
Average in the 2010s, the lowest decade

points.h: Rates climbed for 30 years, then fell for 40
points.p: The average yield rose from **3.24%** in the 1950s to **10.59%** in the 1980s, more than three times as high. Each decade after that was lower, down to **2.41%** in the 2010s. The 2020s so far, at **3.1%**, have edged back up.

points.h: From 1990 to 2019 the yield mostly drifted down
points.p: The yearly average went from **8.55%** in 1990 to **2.14%** in 2019, about a quarter of where it began. The lowest year in this period was 2012, at **1.8%**. There were small rises along the way, such as 2018 at 2.91%.

points.h: All ten highest years fall between 1979 and 1990
points.p: The top year was 1981 at **13.91%**, followed by 1982 at **13%**. Eight of the ten highest years were in the 1980s. The other two were 1979 and 1990, so the period of very high rates was fairly short.

story.note: The yield is the yearly return on lending to the US government for 10 years; the numbers are yearly averages of monthly figures.

q: Which countries have the most people?

queries.purpose: Top 15 countries by population in 2025 (millions of people)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, ROUND(population / 1e6, 1) AS value FROM population WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2025 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Top 15 countries by population in 1960 for comparison (millions of people)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, ROUND(population / 1e6, 1) AS value FROM population WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 1960 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Population growth 1960 to 2025 for the 2025 top 10 countries (millions of extra people)
queries.sql: WITH top AS (SELECT country_code FROM population WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2025 ORDER BY population DESC LIMIT 10) SELECT p25.country AS label, ROUND((p25.population - p60.population) / 1e6, 1) AS value FROM population p25 JOIN population p60 ON p25.country_code = p60.country_code AND p60.year = 1960 WHERE p25.year = 2025 AND p25.country_code IN (SELECT country_code FROM top) ORDER BY value DESC

story.lead: India and China have the most people.
story.summary: India is now the most populous country, with **1,463.9 million** people, just ahead of China at **1,406.6 million**. Each has more than four times the people of the United States (**341.8 million**), which is third. In 1960 China was clearly first, with India far behind.
story.sub: World Bank population figures for countries (not regions or groups), 2025 compared with 1960.

points.h: India and China are far ahead of everyone else
points.p: India has **1,463.9 million** people and China **1,406.6 million**. The United States in third place has **341.8 million**, so each giant is more than four times its size. Indonesia, Pakistan and Nigeria follow.

points.h: In 1960, China led and India was well behind
points.p: China had **667.1 million** people in 1960 and India **436 million**. The list then included Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, France and Ukraine, which are not among the 2025 top 15. Pakistan and Nigeria were near the bottom of the list.

points.h: India added the most people, over a billion
points.p: India grew by **1,027.9 million** people between 1960 and 2025, and China by **739.5 million**. Pakistan, Indonesia and Nigeria each added close to 200 million or more. Russia added only **23.6 million**.

story.note: Figures are World Bank estimates for 2025, and only countries are ranked, not regions or groups of countries.

q: How cheap is natural gas now?

queries.purpose: Recent monthly Henry Hub gas price, last 24 months
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(month, '%b %Y') AS label, ROUND(usd_per_mmbtu, 2) AS value FROM (SELECT month, usd_per_mmbtu FROM gas_prices ORDER BY month DESC LIMIT 24) ORDER BY month

queries.purpose: Average price per year since 1997 for context (2026 so far)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) AS value FROM gas_prices GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Latest month compared with the highest-priced years, to show where now sits
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Latest month (' || strftime(MAX(month), '%b %Y') || ')' AS label, ROUND(arg_max(usd_per_mmbtu, month), 2) AS value FROM gas_prices UNION ALL SELECT 'Average since 1997', ROUND(AVG(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) FROM gas_prices UNION ALL SELECT 'Median since 1997', ROUND(median(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) FROM gas_prices UNION ALL SELECT 'Cheapest month ever (' || strftime(arg_min(month, usd_per_mmbtu), '%b %Y') || ')', ROUND(MIN(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) FROM gas_prices UNION ALL SELECT 'Most expensive month (' || strftime(arg_max(month, usd_per_mmbtu), '%b %Y') || ')', ROUND(MAX(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) FROM gas_prices) ORDER BY value DESC

story.lead: Natural gas is fairly cheap now, but not a record low.
story.summary: In August 2026 US natural gas cost **$2.78** per million BTU (a standard unit of energy). That is about a third below the average since 1997 (**$4.09**) and below the typical month (**$3.40**). It is still almost twice the cheapest month ever (**$1.49**, March 2024).
story.sub: Henry Hub spot price, US Energy Information Administration, monthly, January 1997 to August 2026 (2026 is a partial year).

facts.label: Latest price, Aug 2026, per million BTU

points.h: Prices have settled near $3 after a January spike
points.p: Over the last 24 months the price mostly stayed between about **$2.20** and **$4.30**. January 2026 stands out at **$7.72**, but it fell back to **$3.62** the next month. By August 2026 it was **$2.78**, close to the lowest level since late 2024.

points.h: This year's average is in the middle of the pack
points.p: Yearly averages have ranged from **$2.03** in 2020 to **$8.86** in 2008. The 2026 average so far is **$3.61**, but it is pulled up by the January spike. Recent months have run lower than that.

points.h: Today's price is below the long-run norm
points.p: The latest month, **$2.78**, sits under both the average (**$4.09**) and the median (**$3.40**). The median is the middle month when all months are lined up by price. The peak was **$13.42** in October 2005, almost five times today's price.

story.note: Prices are in current US dollars and not adjusted for inflation, so older prices would look different in today's money.

story.lead: Lebanon's prices rose fastest recently, up 221%.
story.summary: Lebanon had the highest recent inflation: prices rose **221.3%** in 2023, so prices were about three times their level a year earlier. That is more than four times the 2023 rate in Turkiye (**53.9%**), the next country in 2023. The all-time record is far higher: **23,773%** in Congo (Dem. Rep.) in 1994.
story.sub: World Bank consumer price data, 1960–2024; recent ranking uses each country's latest year from 2022 on.

facts.label: Lebanon's price rise in 2023, the highest recently
Sudan's price rise in 2022, second on the recent list

points.h: Lebanon, Sudan and Zimbabwe top the recent list
points.p: This ranks each country by its latest year from 2022 on, so the years differ. Lebanon (**221.3%** in 2023), Sudan (**138.8%**, 2022) and Zimbabwe (**104.7%**, 2022) are the only three above 100%. Turkiye follows at **58.5%** in 2024.

points.h: In 2023 alone, Lebanon stands far above the rest
points.p: Looking only at 2023, when nearly all countries have data, Lebanon's **221.3%** is more than four times Turkiye's **53.9%**. Suriname (**51.6%**) and Sierra Leone (**47.6%**) come next. By the 15th place, Sao Tome and Principe, prices still rose **21.3%**.

points.h: The worst years on record were far more extreme
points.p: Congo (Dem. Rep.) hit **23,773%** in 1994, and Bolivia **11,750%** in 1985. That means prices in Congo were roughly 240 times their level a year earlier. Most of the worst years were in the 1980s and 1990s.

q: Which US cities saw the biggest house price rises?

queries.purpose: Price rise since January 2000 to each city's latest month, top 20 cities
queries.sql: SELECT regexp_replace(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-', '') AS label, round(arg_max("index", month) - 100, 0) AS value FROM us_house_prices WHERE regexp_matches(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-') GROUP BY area ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 20

queries.purpose: Price rise over the last 10 years (latest month vs 10 years earlier), top 20 cities
queries.sql: WITH last AS (SELECT area, max(month) AS m FROM us_house_prices WHERE regexp_matches(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-') GROUP BY area) SELECT regexp_replace(l.area, '^[A-Z]{2}-', '') AS label, round((n."index" / o."index" - 1) * 100, 0) AS value FROM last l JOIN us_house_prices n ON n.area = l.area AND n.month = l.m JOIN us_house_prices o ON o.area = l.area AND o.month = l.m - INTERVAL 10 YEAR ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 20

queries.purpose: Price rise over the last 5 years (latest month vs 5 years earlier), top 20 cities
queries.sql: WITH last AS (SELECT area, max(month) AS m FROM us_house_prices WHERE regexp_matches(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-') GROUP BY area) SELECT regexp_replace(l.area, '^[A-Z]{2}-', '') AS label, round((n."index" / o."index" - 1) * 100, 0) AS value FROM last l JOIN us_house_prices n ON n.area = l.area AND n.month = l.m JOIN us_house_prices o ON o.area = l.area AND o.month = l.m - INTERVAL 5 YEAR ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 20

story.lead: Los Angeles, Miami and San Diego lead since 2000

facts.label: Los Angeles price rise since Jan 2000
Miami price rise over the last 10 years

points.h: Los Angeles, Miami and San Diego have risen most since 2000

points.h: Over 10 years, Miami, Tampa and Charlotte lead
